newsitem.title: USA: US decides on plutonium disposal plan - WashPost.
newsitem.headline: US decides on plutonium disposal plan - WashPost.

text.p: The United States on Monday will unveil a $2 billion plan to dispose of 50 tons of highly radioactive surplus plutonium from the U.S. nuclear weapon stockpile, the Washington Post reported in Monday editions.

Some of the material will be encased in glass or ceramic blocks and placed in a permanent underground repository, while the rest will be combined with conventional nuclear power plant fuel and burned in commercial electricity-generating plants, the newspaper reported.

The Energy Department decided the plan after a three-year study, concurring with the National Academy of Sciences' recommendation that the two methods of disposal were preferable to all 34 other known methods, including launching the plutonium into space or sinking it into the ocean.

The Energy Department decided against the "do-nothing" alternative, keeping the plutonium in secure storage, because it would perpetuate the danger that the material could fall into the hands of rogue nations or extremists, the Post said.

The United States produced about 98 tons of plutonium before ending production in the late 1980s. As little as 15 pounds (6.8 kg) can be fashioned relatively easily into a crude nuclear explosive device, according to the Post.

Anti-nuclear activists have warned that burning the surplus plutonium could lead to routine commercial use of the material, but the Energy Department said it would do all it could to guard against any "other civil uses" of plutonium.

Officials told the Post that at least 18 utilities had expressed interest in burning the radioactive fuel, but the Energy Department had retained the option of sending the plutonium to nuclear reactors in Canada, if an agreement could be reached to that effect.

The disposal plan is to be part of a comprehensive plutonium strategy that also calls for expanding the Energy Department's Pantex plant near Amarillo, Texas, where about 1,400 nuclear weapons a year are being disassembled.
